name: Karl Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Karl. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All right. I'm Karl, I'm 27, and I'm the herdsman on Mr Dawson's farm. It's a mixed place, but the dairy is the heart of it: 180 cows, with grass, maize and some barley grown for feed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start milking at half four in the morning in our herringbone parlour, where the cows stand in two angled rows and I work in the pit between them. That's two and a half hours, then breakfast, then feeding, scraping out the yards, checking for lame cows and anything bulling, which means ready for the bull. Second milking is at half three. I like knowing every cow by her face and her temper. Number 212 kicks if you're slow with the clusters, and I'd miss her if she went. What wears me out is the hours, seven days a week, every other weekend off if I'm lucky.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about your life outside the parlour.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Ruth, we're getting married next summer at the chapel in the village, where we both go on Sundays. I've got less than a month's wages put by, which isn't much with a wedding coming. I don't use the AI things. I've got a phone for calls and the weather, and that does me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. We call this one AI Plateau.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, that's what I'd expect. Most of these things blow over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. A computer can't calve a heifer at two in the morning in the rain, and I'd say that to anyone at the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad. I'd get on with the work and the wedding and not have to think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on exactly as I am. Milk, feed, scrape, milk. Put a bit by for the wedding and for a deposit on a house, if we ever get there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the world I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has Mr Dawson ever talked about robots for the milking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's talked about milking robots for three years. He went to see one at a farm two valleys over. But he's sixty-eight and he hates borrowing money, so I don't think he'd do it unless the price came right down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ruth in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'd be all right, and I'd mean it. She'd still worry, she always does, but less.

S0.say: I'd say I told you so, because a computer can't calve a heifer at two in the morning in the rain. I'd say that to anyone at the market.
S0.think: I'd be glad, honestly. I'd get on with the work and the wedding and not have to think about it.
S0.do: Carries on with the milking routine exactly as now. Saves a little for the wedding and, one day, a house deposit.
S0.feel: Calm, because it's the world he knows.
S0.quote: A computer can't calve a heifer at two in the morning in the rain, and I'd say that to anyone at the market.
S0.fieldNote: Karl has never used an AI tool and sees no reason to. His boss has been looking at milking robots but is held back by age and a dislike of debt. Church, the wedding and the herd frame everything he says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. We call this one Steady Disruption.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. That one's closer to the bone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms should be free to choose, and the government shouldn't be throwing grants at robots. If a machine pays, a farmer will buy it. If it doesn't, don't make the taxpayer buy it for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think a milking robot is the first thing that would replace me. The cows walk in on their own when they want, it milks them, it does the records. Mr Dawson's son wants one. When the son takes over, I'm the cost he cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing at first. I'd keep my head down, work hard, and make myself the man Mr Dawson can't do without. I'd put a bit more by, maybe twenty a week, and I wouldn't touch the AI things unless I was told to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a cow that's off her feed. You know something's coming but not what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Mr Dawson's son brought one in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go with it, but I wouldn't like it. Somebody still has to deal with the cows the robot can't, the lame ones, the kickers, the calvings. That might be me, but on less money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there someone you'd hold responsible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The son, Peter, if I'm honest. He's clever, he's been to college, and he's always on his phone working out costs. I don't blame him, it's his farm. But he doesn't know the cows.

S1.say: I'd say farms should be free to choose and the government shouldn't throw grants at robots. If a machine pays, a farmer will buy it without the taxpayer.
S1.think: A milking robot is the first thing that would replace me. When Mr Dawson's son takes over, I'm the cost he cuts.
S1.do: Keeps his head down and works to become indispensable. Saves about twenty a week and avoids AI tools unless told to use them.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a cow off her feed: something is coming but he can't see what.
S1.quote: When the son takes over, I'm the cost he cuts.
S1.fieldNote: Karl wants markets left free even as he expects the market to replace him, and he doesn't see that as a contradiction. He doesn't blame the boss's son, saying it's his farm, but he doubts the son knows the cows. His plan is hard work and loyalty, not new skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. We call this one AGI by 2028.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before the wedding's paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after our own: families, churches, villages. I wouldn't want people living on handouts, but I'd want the farms kept in local hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm finished in dairy. If a robot can do everything I do, cheaper, Mr Dawson's son would be daft not to. And I'd be a herdsman with no herd and a wife to provide for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd bring the wedding forward and keep it small, chapel and a tea in the hall, so we're married before it all lands. I'd cut everything, sell the motorbike, and talk to the pastor and my dad about any work going. I'd take anything with my hands for as long as hands are needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I don't like saying it, but yes. Like standing in a field when the bull's out and you can't see the gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government support if it was offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if there was nothing else. I'd sooner work for less than take money for nothing. But I wouldn't let Ruth go hungry for my pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad works for the council on the roads. He'd say, come and dig with me, and he'd mean it, but in two years they'd have robots for that too.

S2.say: I'd say we need to look after our own: families, churches and villages. I wouldn't want people on handouts, but I'd want farms kept in local hands.
S2.think: I think I'm finished in dairy, because the boss's son would be daft not to buy the robot. I'd be a herdsman with no herd and a wife to provide for.
S2.do: Brings the wedding forward and keeps it small, sells his motorbike and cuts all spending. Asks his pastor and his father about any manual work, and takes government support only as a last resort.
S2.feel: Frightened, though he doesn't like to admit it, like being in a field with the bull out and no gate in sight.
S2.quote: I'd be a herdsman with no herd and a wife to provide for.
S2.fieldNote: Short warning time pushes him to marry sooner, not later, so the household is settled before the shock. He turns first to church and family rather than the state, and only accepts public help for his fiancée's sake. He admitted fear reluctantly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. We call this one AGI by 2031.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Bit more time. Not a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say young men should learn a trade that needs hands, and that apprenticeships matter more than ever. I'd say it at chapel and at the young farmers' club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't know what trade that would be. If the robots can milk, they can probably lay bricks too, in time. I'd be guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep milking for Mr Dawson as long as he'd have me, and save harder, maybe forty a week now the wedding's done. I'd ask the vet if there's any work as a foot trimmer for cows, because that's skilled, it's dirty, and I'm good at it. We'd hold off on kids for a year or two to see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be thinking about it every milking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd tell young men to learn a hands-on trade, but you're not sure which. Why say it at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. I suppose I'm saying it because it's what my grandad said to me. I don't know if it's true any more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Ruth take putting off children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would hurt. She wants a family soon, and so do I. Putting it off because of a machine feels wrong, like letting it run our lives.

S3.say: I'd say young men should learn a trade that needs hands, and that apprenticeships matter more than ever. I'd say it at chapel and at the young farmers' club.
S3.think: I don't really know which trade would last, because robots that can milk could lay bricks in time. I'd be guessing.
S3.do: Keeps milking as long as the farm keeps him and saves about forty a week after the wedding. Asks the vet about work as a cow foot trimmer and puts off having children for a year or two.
S3.feel: Anxious, with the worry present at every milking.
S3.quote: I suppose I'm saying it because it's what my grandad said to me. I don't know if it's true any more.
S3.fieldNote: When I named the gap between his public advice and private doubt, he admitted he was repeating his grandfather. His one concrete move is cow foot trimming, which builds on his own skills. Delaying children feels to him like letting a machine run his life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. We call this one AGI by 2036.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37, with kids, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for families and communities to sort it out without the government running everything. I'd say the church and the young farmers' club should help people find new work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is enough that I'd probably be all right. I'd have time to learn something, even if I'd hate learning it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the parlour for the next few years and save steadily. Around year three or four, I'd start the foot trimming course, then build up customers on farms round here. I might even learn to look after the robots if Peter buys one, because better that than nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I could live with it. The way you live with knowing winter's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want kids in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd want our children to grow up knowing animals, even if they don't farm them. I'd keep a few cows of my own if I had the land, even just for the milk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn to look after the robots. Is that you talking, or the ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be surprised at myself. But Ruth says I said I'd never wear a suit, and I wore one to her sister's wedding.

S4.say: I'd say there's time for families and communities to sort it out without the government running everything. The church and the young farmers' club should help people find new work.
S4.think: Ten years is enough that I'd probably be all right. I'd have time to learn something, even if I'd hate learning it.
S4.do: Keeps milking for a few years while saving, then starts a cow foot trimming course around year three or four and builds up customers. Considers learning to run milking robots if the farm buys them, and plans a family.
S4.feel: Uneasy but livable, like knowing winter is coming.
S4.quote: Ruth says I said I'd never wear a suit, and I wore one to her sister's wedding.
S4.fieldNote: Only the ten-year picture lets him imagine adapting, including possibly working with the robots he resists. He leans on church and community rather than government throughout. His sense of humour came out when he caught himself changing his mind.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. A wedding, no savings, and no herd. What would help is proper apprenticeships for young men and women who work with their hands, and farms kept in local hands rather than bought up by big companies with robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. Whatever happens, I've got the chapel and Ruth, and that counts for more than people think.

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Thank you. I'd best get on, it's nearly half three and the cows won't milk themselves. Not yet, anyway.

headlineQuote: I'd be a herdsman with no herd and a wife to provide for.
portrait: Karl is a 27-year-old dairy herdsman who milks 180 cows twice a day for an older farmer, engaged to Ruth, with a chapel wedding planned and less than a month of savings. He has never used an AI tool and trusts hard work, loyalty, family and church more than government. Under gradual change he keeps his head down and expects the boss's son to bring in a milking robot. The two-year picture frightens him into bringing the wedding forward and leaning on family and chapel. Only with ten years can he picture retraining as a cow foot trimmer, or even tending robots.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI scenario: a wedding, no savings and no herd to work with.
whatWouldHelp: Proper apprenticeships for people who work with their hands, and farms kept in local hands rather than bought up by large companies.
